## Welcome {#home}

### Stroke

**Learning Objectives:**

- Describe the descriptive epidemiology of stroke
- Distinguish ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke and explain why the
  distinction matters for treatment
- Apply the FAST test for community-level stroke recognition
- Identify major and other risk factors for stroke
- Apply primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention to stroke
- Explain why stroke mortality has declined in some countries

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
Stroke risk factors overlap heavily with coronary artery disease (CAD)
and with hypertension (previous module) — this module emphasizes that
overlap rather than treating stroke as an isolated condition.
:::

---

## Descriptive Epidemiology {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

**Stroke (cerebrovascular disease)** — sudden loss of brain function due
to a vascular lesion; a leading cause of death and a major source of
disability and economic impact. Can occur in children, though with
different risk factors than adult stroke.

- **Age:** the strongest determinant — incidence roughly doubles each
  decade after age 55; mortality also rises with age
- **Sex:** higher incidence in males
- **Time trend:** a striking decline in stroke mortality in many
  countries, attributed mainly to better hypertension control, secondary
  prevention after TIA, reduced smoking, and improved acute treatment

---

## Types of Stroke {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Stroke is not a single pathology — the two broad types share risk
factors but differ in mechanism, and this distinction determines
emergency management (e.g. thrombolysis is appropriate only in
ischaemic stroke):

- **Ischaemic stroke (~85% of cases)** — blood supply to part of the
  brain is blocked, most often by a **thrombus** (local clot, usually
  atherosclerotic) or an **embolus** (a clot travelling from elsewhere,
  classically the heart in atrial fibrillation)
- **Haemorrhagic stroke (~15% of cases)** — bleeding into or around
  brain tissue, split into:
  - **Intracerebral haemorrhage** — bleeding directly into brain
    tissue, most strongly linked to poorly controlled hypertension
  - **Subarachnoid haemorrhage** — bleeding into the space around the
    brain, classically from a ruptured berry aneurysm

**Why the distinction matters for prevention:** hypertension drives
both types, but antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy — a tertiary
prevention tool for ischaemic stroke — would worsen a haemorrhagic
stroke, which is why accurate early diagnosis (imaging) precedes any
tertiary-level treatment decision.

---

## Recognizing a Stroke: The FAST Test {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Because acute stroke treatment (thrombolysis) is highly time-sensitive,
community-level recognition is itself a public health intervention —
this is the population-education counterpart to Chapter 28's health-talk
skills, applied to stroke:

- **F — Face:** ask the person to smile; look for facial drooping on
  one side
- **A — Arms:** ask them to raise both arms; look for one arm drifting
  downward
- **S — Speech:** ask them to repeat a simple sentence; listen for
  slurred or strange speech
- **T — Time:** if any sign is present, note the time symptoms started
  and seek emergency care immediately — "time is brain"

**Why this belongs in a prevention framework:** rapid recognition and
transport is what makes tertiary-level treatment (thrombolysis,
rehabilitation) possible at all — a stroke unrecognized at home never
reaches the acute care where outcomes are actually changed.

---

## Risk Factors {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Stroke risk factors are **largely shared with coronary artery disease**
— this overlap is the single most testable fact about stroke
epidemiology:

- **Major:** hypertension (the single most important risk factor),
  smoking, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes mellitus, heart disease,
  polycythaemia, thrombocythaemia
- **Other:** family history, oral contraceptive use, previous
  stroke/TIA, carotid bruit, obesity, physical inactivity, high alcohol
  intake, drug abuse, trauma, coexisting CAD or peripheral vascular
  disease

---

## Prevention {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Applying the standard levels-of-prevention framework (Chapter 2) to
stroke specifically:

| Level | Action |
|---|---|
| **Primary** | Detect and control risk factors — especially hypertension, smoking, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, heart disease, TIA |
| **Secondary** | Early detection (no definitive screening test exists; carotid bruit auscultation in high-risk individuals is reasonable); low-dose aspirin has a suggested but not firmly proven role |
| **Tertiary** | Acute treatment — rehabilitation, anticoagulants in selected cases; preventing recurrence — antiplatelet therapy, carotid endarterectomy in selected cases |

**Exam tip:** unlike cancer or diabetes, stroke has **no established
population screening test** — prevention relies almost entirely on
controlling upstream risk factors (primary prevention), which is why
hypertension control gets so much emphasis.

The single most important risk factor for stroke is:

## Self-Check: Question 1a {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1a

Thrombolysis is an appropriate emergency treatment for which type of
stroke?

- Subarachnoid haemorrhage
- Intracerebral haemorrhage
- [Ischaemic stroke]{.correct data-explanation="Thrombolysis dissolves a clot blocking a vessel, which is appropriate only for ischaemic stroke (~85% of cases); giving it in a haemorrhagic stroke would worsen the bleeding, which is why imaging to distinguish the two precedes any treatment decision."}
- All types equally
:::

- Malaria

## Self-Check: Question 3 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

### Question 3

Which statement about stroke screening is correct?

- A validated population-wide screening test exists and should be applied to all adults
- [No definitive early-detection test exists; prevention relies primarily on controlling upstream risk factors]{.correct data-explanation="Unlike some cancers or diabetes, there is no established screening test for stroke — this is why primary prevention (risk factor control) carries so much of the preventive burden."}
